What happens when a premium air purifier’s cloud service goes down? The Coway Airmega IconS, a Wi‑Fi‑enabled model, relies entirely on Coway’s proprietary API, leaving users without control during outages.

The author notes the cloud fails “once or twice a year,” sometimes banning the Home Assistant integration or causing days‑long loss of remote control. The device never opens a local network port, so every status poll and command must travel through a TLS‑encrypted connection to Coway’s servers.

When the app was rebranded from IoCare to IoCare+, and the HTML layout it scrapes changed, the community integration had to be rewritten each time. These shifts forced users to monitor updates and redeploy configurations just to keep the fan responsive.

“Cloud dependence makes reliable automation a practical obstacle.”  

Reliance on a third‑party service means a single outage can break a “Good Night” scene that dims lights and starts the fan, undermining the whole smart home experience.

The solution described replaces the cloud layer with a self‑hosted MQTT bridge that emulates the Coway API, allowing direct LAN control and eliminating latency and bans.

Would you consider moving any of your IoT devices to a local‑only setup to avoid similar issues?
